title: Fire
hook: a monk cuts a hole in a perfectly good mat and hangs it in front of a fire. why?
tomorrow: how do you look at something you can't see?

segments.voice: Yesterday's object sat still in a bowl: clear water, the disc after earth in Buddhaghosa's list. Today's object never sits still at all.

Birthday candles get a few seconds of attention before somebody blows them out. A campfire gets longer: a whole circle of friends goes quiet, phones down, watching nothing but the flame. An old meditation manual, Buddhaghosa's Path of Purification, takes that stare and turns it into a practice, and it begins with a strange bit of craft. A monk splits damp wood and lets it dry. He builds a fire in a sheltered spot. Then he takes a mat, or a piece of leather, or cloth, cuts a round hole in it, and hangs it between himself and the fire. He sits down facing the hole. Why ruin a perfectly good mat?
screen: `A CIRCLE OF FRIENDS GOES QUIET.` → `A MAT WITH A HOLE IN IT.` → `WHY RUIN A GOOD MAT?`

segments.voice: Because the hole is a frame. Buddhaghosa is precise about what to leave out. Not the grass and sticks at the bottom, where the fire is fed. Not the smoke curling off the top. Take the thick middle of the flame, he says, and stay there. Don't dwell on its color or its heat. Hold only the name: fire. Tejo, in Pali. What comes next comes in stages. At first the image is restless, like bits of flame breaking off and dropping away. With patience a steadier sign can appear, and his pictures for it are lovely: a piece of red cloth hanging still in space, a golden fan, a golden column. Then a surprising aside. Someone who did this practice before, in an earlier life as the tradition tells it, may need no mat at all. A lamp flame, a fire in an oven, a forest burning in the distance can be enough. Now notice what the mat doesn't do. It doesn't put the fire out or clear away the smoke. The sticks are still crackling. Everything else is still there; it just isn't the object. That's the craft: not fighting the noise, but choosing a frame and resting inside it.
screen: `THE HOLE IS A FRAME.` · `NOT THE STICKS, NOT THE SMOKE.` · `RESTLESS, THEN STILL, LIKE RED CLOTH.` · `THE NOISE STAYS. IT'S NOT THE OBJECT.` · then, large: `THE FLAME.`

segments.voice: If you have a candle and it's safe to light, light it; if not, a lamp or any small glow will do. Let your eyes rest on the bright middle, not the wick and not what rises above it. When your mind drifts, say fire, quietly, and come back to the middle.
Fire: tejo in Pali. A flame seen through a hole in a screen, so its bright middle is all there is to look at.
Your line: the flame. The sticks and the smoke can stay; they're just outside the frame. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Theravada meditation the fire kasina is taken up with a teacher's guidance, using a flame seen through a round hole in a screen, as Buddhaghosa's Visuddhimagga describes it.

fork.reveal: the mat never puts the fire out. it frames the one part worth watching and lets the rest be.

original.note: Pali: fire, heat. In Buddhaghosa's telling, the plain name held in mind while gazing at the flame.

sources.ref: Visuddhimagga 5 (the fire kasina: dry wood, a screen of mat, leather or cloth with a round hole; leave aside the grass and sticks below and the smoke above; take the sign in the dense middle of the flame; not its color or heat, but the name 'fire'; the learning sign like flame breaking off, the counterpart sign motionless like red cloth in space, a gold fan, a gold column; one with past practice may need only a lamp flame, an oven fire or a forest fire)

notes: Visuddhimagga 5 paraphrased throughout. Confirm the details as told: the screen of mat, leather or cloth with a round hole; leaving aside the grass and sticks below and the smoke above; the dense middle of the flame; not attending to color or heat but to the name tejo; the learning sign's flame fragments; the counterpart sign's similes (red cloth in space, gold fan, gold column); and the aside that one with previous practice may need only a lamp flame, an oven fire or a forest fire. The exact size of the hole is left out on purpose.
